profile.feeling: On top of a surface: the book on the table, the cat on the sofa.

senses.def: on, on top of (touching a surface; Wo? + dative: auf dem Tisch)
at, in (with certain places: auf dem Markt, auf der Post, auf dem Land)

examples.text: Das Buch ist auf dem Tisch.
examples.tr: The book is on the table.

examples.text: Leg das Buch auf den Tisch!
examples.tr: Put the book on the table!

examples.text: Wir kaufen Obst auf dem Markt.
examples.tr: We buy fruit at the market.

examples.text: Wie heißt das auf Deutsch?
examples.tr: What’s that called in German?

profile.synonymsNone: A preposition has no true synonym; the neighbouring prepositions are compared in the pitfalls.

etymology.text: From Middle High German ūf, from Old High German ūf, from Proto-Germanic *upp. Compare Dutch op, English up.

funFacts: auf is English up: aufstehen = to get up, auf! (colloquial) = open.
pitfalls: Two-way preposition: Wo? (where) + dative – Das Buch ist auf dem Tisch; Wohin? (where to) + accusative – Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch.
auf = on a horizontal surface, touching (auf dem Tisch); an = at a side or vertical surface (an der Wand); über = above, not touching (über dem Tisch).
subtleties: Open places take auf, not in: auf dem Markt, auf dem Platz, auf der Straße.

profile.feeling: Hidden below: under the bed, under the sofa.

senses.def: under, below (Wo? + dative: unter dem Bett)

examples.text: Der Schlüssel ist unter dem Sofa.
examples.tr: The key is under the sofa.

examples.text: Die Katze schläft unter dem Tisch.
examples.tr: The cat is sleeping under the table.

examples.text: Das bleibt unter uns!
examples.tr: That stays between us!

collocations.tr: between you and me, among us

profile.synonymsNone: A preposition has no true synonym; the neighbouring prepositions are compared in the pitfalls.

etymology.text: From Middle High German under, unter, from Old High German untar, from Proto-West Germanic *undar. Compare Old Saxon undar, Dutch onder, English under.

funFacts: unter, Dutch onder and English under are one Germanic word.
pitfalls: Two-way preposition: Wo? (where) + dative – Die Tasche ist unter dem Tisch; Wohin? (where to) + accusative – Ich stelle die Tasche unter den Tisch.
Spoken German merges unter dem → unterm (unterm Bett); in writing use unter dem.
subtleties: unter uns gesagt = between you and me.

profile.feeling: Side by side: the lamp next to the bed, the post office next to the bank.

senses.def: next to, beside (Wo? + dative: neben der Tür)
next to (Wohin? + accusative: neben die Tür)

examples.text: Die Lampe steht neben dem Bett.
examples.tr: The lamp is next to the bed.

examples.text: Die Post ist neben der Bank.
examples.tr: The post office is next to the bank.

examples.text: Neben der Arbeit studiert sie noch.
examples.tr: Besides work, she is also studying.

profile.synonymsNone: A preposition has no true synonym; the neighbouring prepositions are compared in the pitfalls.

etymology.text: Inherited from Middle High German nëben, enëben, from Old High German in ebanī (“in a line, level with”). Cognate with Dutch neven, compare English anent.

funFacts: neben hides eben (even, level): “in an even line with”.
pitfalls: Two-way preposition: Wo? (where) + dative – Der Stuhl steht neben dem Tisch; Wohin? (where to) + accusative – Ich stelle den Stuhl neben den Tisch.
subtleties: nebenan (next door) and der Nachbar (neighbour) are handy companions: Mein Nachbar wohnt nebenan.

profile.feeling: In front: the car in front of the house – and, in time, “before” and “ago”.

senses.def: in front of (Wo? + dative: vor dem Haus)
in front of (Wohin? + accusative: vor das Haus)
before (time, + dative: vor dem Essen, vor acht Uhr); ago (vor zwei Jahren)

examples.text: Das Auto steht vor dem Haus.
examples.tr: The car is in front of the house.

examples.text: Wir warten vor dem Kino.
examples.tr: We’re waiting in front of the cinema.

examples.text: Vor dem Essen waschen wir uns die Hände.
examples.tr: Before eating we wash our hands.

examples.text: Vor dem Frühstück trinke ich ein Glas Wasser.
examples.tr: Before breakfast I drink a glass of water.

examples.text: Vor zwei Wochen war ich in Athen.
examples.tr: Two weeks ago I was in Athens.

profile.synonymsNone: A preposition has no true synonym; the neighbouring prepositions are compared in the pitfalls.

etymology.text: From Middle High German vore, vor, from Old High German fora. Cognate with Dutch voor; compare English fore.

funFacts: vor is English fore (before, forehead) and a cousin of Greek πρό (pró).
pitfalls: Two-way preposition: Wo? (where) + dative – Das Auto steht vor dem Haus; Wohin? (where to) + accusative – Ich fahre das Auto vor das Haus.
vor (in front of, before) ≠ für (for): Ich warte vor dem Haus. – Das ist für dich.
In time, vor takes the dative only: vor dem Essen (before the meal), vor acht Uhr (before eight), vor einer Woche (a week ago) – there is no accusative of time.
subtleties: vor + a time = “ago”: vor einer Woche (a week ago) – always dative.
before + a verb is the conjunction bevor (Bevor ich esse, …), not vor.

profile.feeling: At the back: the garden behind the house.

examples.text: Der Garten ist hinter dem Haus.
examples.tr: The garden is behind the house.

examples.text: Die Treppe ist hinter der Tür.
examples.tr: The stairs are behind the door.

examples.text: Das Schlimmste haben wir hinter uns.
examples.tr: We’ve got the worst behind us.

profile.synonymsNone: A preposition has no true synonym; the neighbouring prepositions are compared in the pitfalls.

etymology.text: From Middle High German hinder, from Old High German hintar, from Proto-Germanic *hinder.

funFacts: hinter and English behind / hind (as in hindsight) share the same Germanic root *hind-.
pitfalls: Two-way preposition: Wo? (where) + dative – Der Garten ist hinter dem Haus; Wohin? (where to) + accusative – Wir gehen hinter das Haus.
Spoken German says hinterm (= hinter dem): hinterm Haus.
subtleties: hinter is the opposite of vor; the adverbs are hinten (at the back) and vorne (at the front).

profile.feeling: In the middle of two things – the table between the sofa and the shelf.

senses.def: between (Wo? + dative: zwischen dem Sofa und dem Regal)

examples.text: Der Tisch steht zwischen dem Sofa und dem Regal.
examples.tr: The table is between the sofa and the shelf.

examples.text: Das Café ist zwischen der Bank und der Post.
examples.tr: The café is between the bank and the post office.

examples.text: Zwischen uns ist alles gut.
examples.tr: Everything is fine between us.

profile.synonymsNone: A preposition has no true synonym; the neighbouring prepositions are compared in the pitfalls.

etymology.text: From Old High German in zuiskēn, from zuiski, from Proto-West Germanic *twisk(ī), from Proto-Germanic *twiskaz (“twofold”), from Proto-Indo-European *dwís (“twice”).

funFacts: zwischen contains the old word for “two” (zwei) – like English between (“by two”) and twin.
pitfalls: Two-way preposition: Wo? (where) + dative – zwischen dem Sofa und dem Regal; Wohin? (where to) + accusative – zwischen das Sofa und das Regal. Both nouns take the case.
subtleties: zwischen also works for time: zwischen acht und neun Uhr.

profile.feeling: Close by – just a few steps away.

senses.def: near, close (in time or in a relationship: ein naher Freund)

examples.text: Ist die Apotheke weit? – Nein, sie ist ganz nah.
examples.tr: Is the pharmacy far? – No, it’s very close.

examples.text: Der Bahnhof ist nah am Zentrum.
examples.tr: The station is close to the centre.

examples.text: Weihnachten ist schon nah.
examples.tr: Christmas is already near.

synonyms.nuance: nearby, in the area – the most common way to say it

etymology.text: Inherited from Middle High German nāh, from Old High German nāh. Compare English nigh. Doublet of nach.

funFacts: nah is English nigh (as in “the end is nigh”) – and neighbour is the “nigh-dweller”, German Nachbar.
pitfalls: nah alone or with an/bei: Das Hotel ist nah am Strand. – “Near the station” is more often in der Nähe vom Bahnhof / des Bahnhofs.
Comparison: nah – näher – am nächsten (nächst- also means “next”).
subtleties: nah also means emotionally close: Wir stehen uns sehr nah.

profile.feeling: Somewhere around here – nearby.

senses.def: nearby, in the area; near (in der Nähe von + dative)

examples.text: Ist hier in der Nähe eine Apotheke?
examples.tr: Is there a pharmacy near here?

examples.text: Der Supermarkt ist in der Nähe.
examples.tr: The supermarket is nearby.

examples.text: Wir wohnen in der Nähe vom Bahnhof.
examples.tr: We live near the station.

synonyms.nuance: close – describes the distance (Es ist nah.)

etymology.text: From in (“in”) + der (dative of die) + Nähe (“nearness, vicinity”), from Middle High German næhe, from Old High German nāhī.

funFacts: Nähe and nah are one family – like Greek κοντά and κοντινός.
pitfalls: in der Nähe von + dative: in der Nähe vom Park (von dem → vom).
die Nähe is feminine, so in der Nähe (dative after in).
subtleties: Ist hier in der Nähe …? is the standard question when you look for something.

profile.feeling: A long way – far from home.

senses.def: wide, broad (an adjective: ein weiter Rock)

examples.text: Der Flughafen ist weit.
examples.tr: The airport is far.

examples.text: Ist es weit bis zum Bahnhof?
examples.tr: Is it far to the station?

examples.text: Das Dorf ist nicht weit von hier.
examples.tr: The village isn’t far from here.

examples.text: Die Hose ist zu weit.
examples.tr: The trousers are too wide.

phrases.meaning: everything is fine up to now

etymology.text: From Middle High German wīt, from Old High German wīt, from Proto-Germanic *wīdaz. Compare Dutch wijd, English wide.

funFacts: weit is English wide; English “far” is German fern (as in Fernseher, “far-seer” = TV).
pitfalls: weit means “far” – and “wide”: ein weites Land (a vast country), eine weite Hose (wide trousers).
Far from X: weit von + dative, or weit weg von: weit weg von der Stadt.
subtleties: Wie weit ist es? asks the distance; So weit, so gut = so far, so good.

profile.feeling: Indoors, warm and dry, while it rains outside.

examples.text: Wir essen heute drinnen.
examples.tr: We’re eating inside today.

examples.text: Die Kinder spielen drinnen.
examples.tr: The children are playing indoors.

examples.text: Ist noch jemand drinnen?
examples.tr: Is anybody still inside?

synonyms.nuance: inside, on the inside (of a thing: innen rot = red inside)

etymology.text: From dr- (a short form of dar-) + innen (“inside”).

funFacts: The dr- of drinnen and draußen is a short form of da(r)-: “there-in”, “there-out”.
pitfalls: drinnen is where (Ich bin drinnen); going in is rein / herein (Komm rein!).
subtleties: drinnen is colloquial-neutral and very common; innen is used for the inner side of things (innen und außen).

profile.feeling: Fresh air, the garden, the street – outdoors.

senses.def: out there (far away: draußen auf dem Meer)

examples.text: Die Kinder sind draußen im Garten.
examples.tr: The children are outside in the garden.

examples.text: Draußen ist es kalt.
examples.tr: It’s cold outside.

examples.text: Wir sitzen draußen vor dem Café.
examples.tr: We’re sitting outside the café.

etymology.text: From dr- (a short form of dar-) + außen (“outside”).

funFacts: Draußen nur Kännchen (“outside only pots of coffee”) is a famous sign of old German cafés – a running joke about German rules.
pitfalls: draußen is where you are; going out is nach draußen or raus: Geh raus! / Geh nach draußen!
subtleties: außen is the outer side of something (außen grün); draußen is outdoors.

profile.feeling: Turning left at the corner – and the political left.

senses.def: on the left; to the left

examples.text: Die Küche ist links.
examples.tr: The kitchen is on the left.

examples.text: Gehen Sie hier links!
examples.tr: Turn left here!

examples.text: Sie wählt links.
examples.tr: She votes for the left.

phrases.tr: to do something with the left

synonyms.nuance: on the left-hand side – the longer form

etymology.text: From Middle High German linkes, originally the genitive of linc (whence modern link); by surface analysis link + -s. Cognate with Dutch links.

funFacts: Etwas mit links machen = to do something with ease (literally “with the left”).
pitfalls: links / rechts are adverbs (Die Küche ist links); before a noun use the adjective: die linke Tür, die rechte Hand.
subtleties: Something done “mit links” is done easily – with the left hand, without effort.

profile.feeling: On the right – where Germans walk and drive.

senses.def: on the right; to the right

examples.text: Das Bad ist rechts.
examples.tr: The bathroom is on the right.

examples.text: Die Apotheke ist rechts neben der Bank.
examples.tr: The pharmacy is on the right, next to the bank.

examples.text: Auf der Rolltreppe steht man rechts.
examples.tr: On the escalator you stand on the right.

collocations.tr: right before left (the German priority rule)

synonyms.nuance: on the right-hand side – the longer form

etymology.text: From recht (“right”) + -s (“adverbial suffix”).

funFacts: rechts and recht (right, law) are one word – like English right and Greek δεξιά / δεξιός (right, skilful).
pitfalls: rechts (on the right) is different from recht (right, correct; quite): Du hast recht. – Das ist recht gut.
subtleties: rechts vor links: at crossings without signs, the car coming from the right goes first.

profile.feeling: The heart of the flat – coffee in the morning, cooking in the evening.

examples.text: Meine Mutter ist in der Küche.
examples.tr: My mother is in the kitchen.

examples.text: Die Milch ist im Kühlschrank in der Küche.
examples.tr: The milk is in the fridge in the kitchen.

examples.text: Ich mag die griechische Küche.
examples.tr: I like Greek cuisine.

etymology.text: From Middle High German küche, from Old High German chuhhina, from late Proto-West Germanic *kukinā, from Late Latin cocīna, from earlier coquīna.

funFacts: Küche, kochen and Koch all come from Latin coquere (to cook), like English kitchen and cook.
pitfalls: die Küche (kitchen) vs der Kuchen (cake): Der Kuchen ist in der Küche.
Küche also means cuisine: die deutsche Küche.
subtleties: In German flat adverts, EBK = Einbauküche (fitted kitchen) – many flats are rented without one!

profile.feeling: Tiles, a shower, a mirror – the bathroom.

examples.text: Das Badezimmer ist rechts.
examples.tr: The bathroom is on the right.

examples.text: Die Wohnung hat zwei Badezimmer.
examples.tr: The flat has two bathrooms.

examples.text: Im Badezimmer ist kein Fenster.
examples.tr: There’s no window in the bathroom.

synonyms.nuance: toilet – the room with the WC only

etymology.text: From baden (“to bathe”) + Zimmer (“room”).

funFacts: Zimmer once meant timber (English timber is the same word): a room was what was built of wood.
pitfalls: Asking for the toilet: Wo ist die Toilette? – not *Wo ist das Badezimmer? (that sounds as if you want a shower).
Plural = singular: die Badezimmer; dative plural den Badezimmern.
subtleties: Many German flats have the toilet in the bathroom; a separate WC is called Gäste-WC.

profile.feeling: The bathroom – and a hot bath, a spa town.

senses.def: spa (in town names: Baden-Baden, Bad Ems)

examples.text: Das Bad ist links.
examples.tr: The bathroom is on the left.

examples.text: Die Wohnung hat ein großes Bad.
examples.tr: The flat has a big bathroom.

examples.text: Nach der Arbeit nehme ich ein heißes Bad.
examples.tr: After work I take a hot bath.

synonyms.nuance: the full word for the room

etymology.text: From Middle High German bat, from Old High German bad, from Proto-West Germanic *baþ, from Proto-Germanic *baþą. Related to bähen.

funFacts: Bad is English bath; the city of Bath in England and Baden-Baden in Germany are both named after their hot springs.
pitfalls: Plural with umlaut: die Bäder.
Bad in a town name (Bad Ems, Bad Homburg) means a spa town.
subtleties: In flat adverts Bad is the bathroom; Wanne (tub) or Dusche (shower) says what is in it.

profile.feeling: Quiet and dark – the room with the bed.

examples.text: Das Bett ist im Schlafzimmer.
examples.tr: The bed is in the bedroom.

examples.text: Die Wohnung hat zwei Schlafzimmer.
examples.tr: The flat has two bedrooms.

examples.text: Das Schlafzimmer ist oben, neben dem Bad.
examples.tr: The bedroom is upstairs, next to the bathroom.

synonyms.nuance: children’s room – often also where the children sleep

etymology.text: From Schlaf (“sleep”) + Zimmer (“room”).

funFacts: schlafen (to sleep) is English sleep – Schlafzimmer is literally “sleep room”.
pitfalls: Plural = singular: die Schlafzimmer; dative plural den Schlafzimmern.
German flats are counted in rooms (Zimmer), not bedrooms: eine 3-Zimmer-Wohnung has e.g. two bedrooms and a living room.
subtleties: Schlafzimmerblick (“bedroom look”) is a dreamy, sleepy look.

profile.feeling: Sofa, television, family evenings.

examples.text: Das Sofa ist im Wohnzimmer.
examples.tr: The sofa is in the living room.

examples.text: Wir essen im Wohnzimmer.
examples.tr: We eat in the living room.

examples.text: Das Wohnzimmer hat ein großes Fenster.
examples.tr: The living room has a big window.

collocations.tr: to go into the living room

synonyms.nuance: living room – old-fashioned or regional (gute Stube = the best room)

etymology.text: From wohnen (“to live, reside”) + Zimmer (“room”).

funFacts: Wohnzimmer, Wohnung and wohnen are one family: German “lives” (wohnt) in a Wohnung and sits in the Wohnzimmer.
pitfalls: wohnen = to live (somewhere): Wohnzimmer, Wohnung (flat) – leben = to be alive.
Plural = singular: die Wohnzimmer.
subtleties: die gute Stube was the best room kept for guests in old German homes.

profile.feeling: Flowers, vegetables, a barbecue on summer evenings.

senses.def: orchard; park (in names: der Englische Garten)

examples.text: Die Kinder spielen im Garten.
examples.tr: The children are playing in the garden.

examples.text: Der Garten ist hinter dem Haus.
examples.tr: The garden is behind the house.

examples.text: Mein Opa hat einen Garten mit Tomaten.
examples.tr: My grandpa has a garden with tomatoes.

synonyms.nuance: allotment garden in a colony of small gardens

etymology.text: From Middle High German garte, from Old High German garto, from Proto-West Germanic *gardō. Cognate with English yard, and through French with English garden.

funFacts: The same root gave Russian город (town – once a fenced place) and Turkish has bahçe (from Persian).
pitfalls: der Garten (masculine), plural die Gärten.
im Garten (where) – in den Garten (where to).
subtleties: Kindergarten went into English from German (Friedrich Fröbel, 1840).

profile.feeling: What you walk on – the floor, the ground, the soil.

examples.text: Die Tasche ist auf dem Boden.
examples.tr: The bag is on the floor.

examples.text: Die Kinder sitzen auf dem Boden.
examples.tr: The children are sitting on the floor.

examples.text: Der Boden hier ist sehr gut für Kartoffeln.
examples.tr: The soil here is very good for potatoes.

collocations.tr: on the floor, on the ground

synonyms.nuance: floor – only the floor of a room

etymology.text: From Middle High German boden, bodem, from Old High German bodam, from Proto-West Germanic *bodm. Cognate with English bottom, Dutch bodem.

funFacts: Boden is English bottom; the Bodensee (Lake Constance) is named after the old palace of Bodman.
pitfalls: Plural with umlaut: die Böden.
auf dem Boden = on the floor; “floor” as a storey is der Stock / die Etage: im ersten Stock.
subtleties: Boden has many senses: floor, ground, soil, bottom, attic – the context decides.

profile.feeling: The surface of a room you walk on – wood, tiles, carpet.

examples.text: Das Handy liegt auf dem Fußboden.
examples.tr: The phone is lying on the floor.

examples.text: Der Fußboden ist aus Holz.
examples.tr: The floor is made of wood.

examples.text: In der Küche sind die Fußböden aus Stein.
examples.tr: In the kitchen the floors are made of stone.

etymology.text: From Fuß (“foot”) + Boden (“bottom, ground, floor”).

funFacts: Fußbodenheizung (underfloor heating) – a very long and very German word for a very comfortable thing.
pitfalls: Plural with umlaut: die Fußböden.
In Switzerland it is written Fussboden.
subtleties: Fußboden is more precise than Boden: only the floor of a room, never soil or attic.

profile.feeling: Up and down – the stairs in the hallway.

examples.text: Die Treppe ist hinter der Tür.
examples.tr: The stairs are behind the door.

examples.text: Das Kind sitzt auf der Treppe.
examples.tr: The child is sitting on the stairs.

examples.text: Wir nehmen die Treppe, nicht den Aufzug.
examples.tr: We take the stairs, not the lift.

synonyms.nuance: stairs – the Austrian and Bavarian word

etymology.text: Attested since the 12th century, from Middle High German treppe, trappe, from Old High German trappa, from Proto-West Germanic *trappā.

funFacts: Treppenwitz is a calque of French l’esprit de l’escalier, “staircase wit”.
pitfalls: German says die Treppe (singular) for “the stairs”: Die Treppe ist steil.
One step is die Stufe.
subtleties: Treppenwitz: the clever reply you think of too late, on the stairs going out (French l’esprit de l’escalier).

profile.feeling: Books, plants, photos – the shelf unit on the wall.

examples.text: Die Bücher sind im Regal.
examples.tr: The books are on the shelf.

examples.text: Das Regal steht neben dem Fenster.
examples.tr: The shelf unit is next to the window.

examples.text: Im Supermarkt sind die Regale voll.
examples.tr: In the supermarket the shelves are full.

etymology.text: Early 17th century, of unclear origin; perhaps related to Reihe (“row”) or to Latin rēgula (“bar, rule”).

funFacts: IKEA’s Billy is the classic German student bookcase – Billy-Regal.
pitfalls: Things are IM Regal (inside the unit), not *auf dem Regal – unless they lie on top of it.
Plural die Regale.
subtleties: Regal is the whole unit; a single shelf board is das Regalbrett.

profile.feeling: A lazy evening on the sofa.

examples.text: Der Schlüssel ist unter dem Sofa.
examples.tr: The key is under the sofa.

examples.text: Wir sitzen auf dem Sofa.
examples.tr: We’re sitting on the sofa.

examples.text: Das Sofa steht im Wohnzimmer.
examples.tr: The sofa is in the living room.

synonyms.nuance: couch – very common, also die Couch

etymology.text: 17th century, from French sofa, from Italian sofà, from Ottoman Turkish صفه (sofa), from Arabic صُفَّة (ṣuffa).

funFacts: Sofa travelled from Arabic صُفَّة (a raised bench) via Turkish sofa to Europe – Turkish sofa today is a hall or an entrance room.
pitfalls: das Sofa (neuter), plural die Sofas.
auf dem Sofa sitzen (on), but unter dem Sofa (under).
subtleties: Couch and Sofa mean the same; die Couch is feminine (in Switzerland also der Couch).

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses Kühlschrank as “refrigerator” – the fridge.

profile.feeling: Cold milk, butter, leftovers – open the door and look.

examples.text: Die Milch ist im Kühlschrank.
examples.tr: The milk is in the fridge.

examples.text: Der Kühlschrank ist leer!
examples.tr: The fridge is empty!

examples.text: Stell die Butter in den Kühlschrank.
examples.tr: Put the butter in the fridge.

synonyms.nuance: icebox – the old word, still heard from older people

etymology.text: From kühl (“cool”) + Schrank (“cupboard, cabinet”).

funFacts: Kühlschrank is built like Greek ψυγείο (from ψύχω, to cool): named after the cold, not after the food.
pitfalls: im Kühlschrank (where: dative) – in den Kühlschrank (where to: accusative).
Plural with umlaut: die Kühlschränke.
subtleties: Kühlschrank is literally “cool cupboard”; a freezer is der Gefrierschrank or das Gefrierfach.
